newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo iron and steel output seen rising sharply.
newsitem.headline: Yugo iron and steel output seen rising sharply.

text.p: Yugoslav ferrous metals producers expect output to rise by 60 percent in 1997 despite daunting insolvency and low domestic demand.

"Overall output of the ferrous metals industry can rise even by 60 percent this year if we maintain the production trend of the last quarter of 1996," Arsenije Jovanovic, director of the Yugoslav Iron and Steel Federation said.
Jovanovic said that the set production target would be very difficult to achieve considering current insolvency in the banking system, lack of working capital and low local demand.
"But we hope for financial help from our partners abroad," he said in an interview with Reuters.
"Interest obviously exists as we already have some concrete offers," the director said, but declined to go into detail.
Almost four years of international sanctions against Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, brought iron and steel production, like the entire country's economy, almost to a standstill.

The ferrous metals sector was among the few industries to recover and almost reach the pre-sanctions 1991 level. But according to Jovanovic, output was still slightly below 1989 when production was at its height.

The results were satisfactory, he said, considering that furnaces in Serbia's Smederevo and Montenegro's Niksic steel mills were lit only in April last year thanks to credit lines secured from their traditional partners from abroad.
Pig iron output stood at 568,000 tonnes in 1996 against 108,000 tonnes the previous year. Production in 1991 was 525,000 tonnes and 881,000 tonnes in 1989.
Total production of crude steel was 685,000 tonnes in 1996 compared to 182,000 tonnes the previous year. In 1991, the output was 715,000 tonnes and 1.15 million tonnes in 1989.
Jovanovic praised export results saying that as much as 60 percent of the total iron and steel production went to foreign markets.
"This is a remarkable success considering severe international competition," he said adding that this year's export target was 70 percent of the overall output.
Yugoslavia exported 330,000 tonnes of crude steel in 1996.

According to Jovanovic, imports stood at 231,000 tonnes out of which about 88 percent was imported from east European countries at dumping prices. "This is an unfair competition and is hurting our industry badly."
He underlined that crude steel imports increased by 41.7 percent in 1996 over 1995 despite a significant increase in local production.
Commodity (finished and semi-finished goods) production reached 738,900 tonnes in 1996, up 197.9 percent from the previous year.
Jovanovic said that exports of 332,000 tonnes of commodity output worth about $100 million was also a great success for the ferrous industry. "This is proof of our return to world markets."
The federation will commission by February a foreign firm to draft a long-term development study to the year 2010 and a privatisation programme for the ferrous industry, he said.
